slides.title: Systems: Which Points Are Solutions; How Many Solutions
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say one line and nothing else yet: “Today: two equations at once — which points make both true.”

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Q4 is today's move: put the x in, get the y. (3, 7) is a point that makes y = 2x + 1 true — say that one sentence after the reveal; Notes I makes a whole line of such points. Two minutes silent, then reveal, no discussion.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Vocabulary
slides.sub: The new words, before they are used.
slides.note: Five words, read once each. Say 'both' twice for the second: a pair that makes one equation true is not a solution of the system. 'Intersect' is the state's word for cross: the point of intersection is the crossing. Parallel is a picture word today — never meet; the coefficient of x is the number that multiplies x (3 in 3x, −1 in −x, 0 in y = 4), and Unit 10 gives it a second name.

slides.title: Notes
slides.sub: Copy the table and the line.
slides.note:
An equation in two letters has many solutions, each an ordered pair. Make a table: x = 0 first, then two more — put each x in and get its y. Plot the three points; they line up, and the line through them holds every solution. Two points draw the line; the third is the check — if it misses, a y is wrong. (1, 3) is a solution because 3 = 1 + 2; (1.5, 3.5) is one too, a point between the grid lines, and so is (100, 102), off the grid. This is the first line this class has drawn from an equation (Unit 10 comes later).
OFF: 'Pick an x, find its y, plot the point. Every point on the line makes the equation true.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Two equations together are a system, and its solution is a pair that makes BOTH true. Put (2, 4) into each: 2 + 2 = 4 and −2(2) + 8 = 4 — a solution. (0, 2) makes the first true and the second not (−2(0) + 8 is 8, not 2) — so it is a solution of y = x + 2 only, and not of the system. On the graph the solution is the point on both lines: where they cross — where they intersect, the point of intersection. (Say nothing today about setting the two expressions equal: 11.07 Notes III shows it.)
OFF: 'A solution of the system makes both equations true. One is not enough.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Three pictures, three counts — read from the picture; the reasons from the equations are 11.07's. Cross once: one solution, the crossing (2, 3). Parallel — they never meet: no solution. The same line — the orange dashes lie on the blue: every point of it is on both graphs, the ones nobody plotted too (infinitely many). These are 11.03's three endings again: one, none, every. Then the level line: y = 3 is a line too — every x gives 3 — so a level line can cross a slanted one, or run parallel to another level line.
OFF: 'Cross once: one. Never meet: none. The same line: infinitely many.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Ask what has to be true of a solution before anyone substitutes: it makes BOTH equations true.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Each pair into each equation. (3, 8): 3(3) − 1 = 8 and 3 + 5 = 8 — both true, a solution. (1, 2) makes the first true and the second not (1 + 5 is 6). (2, 7) makes the second true and the first not (3(2) − 1 is 5). Each wrong pair passes one equation: a board that tested one equation only picked it.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: (2, 7): 2(2) + 3 = 7 and −2 + 9 = 7. (0, 3) passes the first only; (4, 5) passes the second only. A board with (0, 3) or (4, 5) tested one equation.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Ask whether the two lines will ever meet if the grid went on forever, before anyone answers 'how many'.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Read the two lines on the grid at three x's: at x = 0 they are at 2 and −1, at x = 2 at 3 and 0, at x = 4 at 4 and 1 — always 3 apart. Lines that stay 3 apart never meet: parallel, and no pair makes both true. (No algebra today: the reason from the equations is 11.07's.) A board with 'one' guessed the lines meet off the grid; with 'infinitely many', saw two lines going on forever.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: The tables, read column by column: 1 and −3, 5 and 1, 9 and 5 — the first is always 4 more, so the lines stay 4 apart and never meet: no solution. A board with 'one' expects them to meet past the table; with 'infinitely many', read two lines that go on forever.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Both true: yes. A board with 'no' most likely took −4 + 5 as −9 or 9 — ask for the second check aloud.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: The first is true and the second is not, so (2, 5) is not a solution of the system — it is a solution of y = 2x + 1 only. A board with 'yes' stopped after the first equation: today's named misconception.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: The extra-number board (ruling 22): the grid's height, 6, is not needed. Read the crossing on the grid lines: x = −2, y = 3. Then check it in both: −2 + 5 = 3 and 4 − 1 = 3. One crossing, one solution. A board with (3, −2) swapped the coordinates; one with (0, 5) or (0, −1) read where a line meets the y-axis; one with a 6 in it used the grid's height.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. Option C passes the first equation only, option A the second only, and option B is the answer with x and y swapped (it happens to pass the second: −2 + 5 = 3, but 2(2) − 4 = 0). On a split: sixty seconds, convince your neighbor, re-vote — then check (3, 2) in both aloud.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: The pattern breaks: no crossing to read. The same number (1) multiplies x in both, and the added numbers differ, so the first line is always 4 above the second and they never meet. A board with 'one' expects them to meet somewhere off the grid; with 'infinitely many', saw two lines that go on forever.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic on the same-line case, the state's named misconception for AR.4.2; the graph is on the reveal. Every point of the line is on both graphs, the points nobody marked too: (10, 9) is off the grid and makes both true. Option D counts the two marked points; option C looks for a crossing and finds none; option A counts the one line. A and C are the same misreading — the same line taken for something other than every point — and get the same response: point at a third point of the line and check it in both.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: A level line: y = 4 gives 4 for every x, so its graph is flat — 0 multiplies x. It crosses the rising line once, at (3, 4): 3 + 1 = 4, and y = 4 there. A board with 'none' thought a line with no x cannot meet anything; with (4, 3), swapped.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Backwards: x is given and y is missing. Put 2 into each equation; both give 7, so (2, 7) is the solution. Check both — a pair is a solution only if both equations give the same y.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written, and the exit evidence: today's named misconception — a pair that satisfies one equation called a solution of the system. Read two aloud.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Independent Set
slides.sub: Six questions. On your own, in writing.
slides.note: Hand out the Independent Set; the same six questions are on the board. Silent work. Circulate and mark what you see; do not teach. Whatever is not finished goes home.
